content: The recommendations drafted by the WHO Steering Group were revised as necessary through group discussions. Each recommendation was finalized by consensus, defined as agreement by at least three-quarters of participants, provided that those who disagreed did not strongly oppose the decision. Any disagreements were resolved during meetings and subsequent exchanges with the Guideline Development Group (GDG) members. No strong disagreements were recorded. If consensus could not be reached, the disputed recommendation or decision would have been subjected to a vote, following the procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. The GDG determined the context of recommendations through the same consensus process, based on discussions about the balance of evidence regarding the benefits and disadvantages of interventions across different contexts, particularly in the setting of rigorous research or targeted monitoring and evaluation. In accordance with WHO procedures for declarations of interest (DOIs), all GDG, Technical Working Group (TWG), and External Review Group (ERG) members, as well as other external collaborators, were required to declare any competing interests (academic, financial, or other) in writing using the standard WHO form before participating in the guideline development process. Experts were instructed to notify the responsible technical officer of any changes in relevant interests during the process to ensure conflicts of interest were updated and reviewed accordingly. Additionally, experts were asked to submit an electronic copy of their curriculum vitae. The WHO Steering Group reviewed all DOI forms and CVs to determine whether any conflicts of interest existed. Findings from the DOI forms were managed on a case-by-case basis in accordance with WHO DOI guidelines. The Steering Group applied criteria from the WHO handbook for guideline development to assess the severity of conflicts of interest. No declared conflicts were deemed serious enough to compromise the guideline development process or its credibility. Therefore, all experts were only required to declare such conflicts at the first GDG meeting. At subsequent virtual GDG meetings, members were required to disclose any new conflicts of interest. Before the final virtual GDG meeting, all GDG and TWG members, as well as observers, were again asked to complete their DOI forms and declare any conflicts to ensure up-to-date information as the recommendations were finalized. Conflicts of interest requiring action by WHO staff arose when experts had conducted primary research or systematic reviews related to any guideline recommendations. In such cases, the experts were restricted from participating in discussions or formulating recommendations in the area of their conflict. A summary of DOIs from the GDG and information on how conflicts of interest were managed are included in Annex 2. The names and short biographies of GDG members were published on the WHO website for public review and comment two weeks before the first GDG meeting. After the final GDG meeting, an independent consultant and WHO technical officers prepared a draft of the full guideline document to accurately reflect the GDG’s deliberations and decisions. Other members of the WHO Steering Group provided comments on the draft before it was sent electronically to GDG members for further input. The document was also sent to the ERG for peer review. ERG members were asked to review the final draft to identify factual errors, comment on language clarity, and provide considerations related to implementation and adaptation. The WHO Steering Group carefully evaluated input from the GDG and peer reviewers for inclusion in the guideline document and made further revisions as needed. After the GDG meetings and external peer review, additional modifications by the Steering Group were limited to correcting factual errors and improving language clarity. A summary of the recommendations is presented in the executive summary of the guideline. For each recommendation, a summary of the evidence on effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, feasibility, and other considerations reviewed at the virtual GDG meetings is provided in Chapter 3. The language used to interpret the evidence on effects aligns with the Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care approach. Implementation of the postnatal care guideline and recommendations is discussed in Chapter 4, with implementation considerations for each GDG recommendation detailed in Web Annex 5. Integrated recommendations and their associated remarks are presented throughout Chapter 3, with references provided in the remarks to indicate the source guideline. For all recommendations, readers are referred to specific WHO guidance for more details, including the evidence base and implementation considerations. This guideline includes 63 evidence-based recommendations on postnatal care, comprising 31 newly developed GDG recommendations and 32 recommendations relevant to postnatal care from previously published WHO guidelines that were integrated into this document. Corresponding GRADE tables for recommendations, referred to as evidence base (EB) tables, are numbered according to the specific recommendations they address and are presented separately in the Web Supplement. Evidence-to-decision tables with GDG judgments related to the evidence and considerations for all domains are presented alongside the summary of evidence and considerations for each recommendation. Summary of judgments tables indicate the final judgment for each domain, with a template summary of judgments showing the range of possible judgment options provided in Annex 3. For maternal assessment, early detection of conditions that may adversely affect postpartum women’s health and well-being, including their ability to care for themselves and their newborns, is a critical component of quality postnatal care. All postpartum women should have regular assessments of vaginal bleeding, uterine tone, fundal height, temperature, and heart rate (pulse) routinely during the first 24 hours, starting from the first hour after birth. Blood pressure should be measured shortly after birth, and if normal, a second measurement should be taken within six hours. Urine voiding should be documented within six hours. At each subsequent postnatal contact beyond 24 hours after birth, inquiries should continue about general well-being, with assessments of micturition and urinary incontinence, bowel function, perineal wound healing, headache, fatigue, back pain, perineal pain and hygiene, breast pain, uterine tenderness, and lochia. In high HIV-burden settings, postpartum HIV testing is recommended for women with HIV-negative or unknown status who missed early antenatal testing or retesting in late pregnancy. In low HIV-burden settings, postpartum HIV testing may be considered for women with ongoing HIV risks, such as those in serodiscordant relationships or with partners not virally suppressed on ART.
